title: Montaigne and La Boetie
text:
In about 1558, at a large public gathering in Bordeaux, Michel de Montaigne met Etienne de La Boetie. Both were young magistrates in the city's parliament. La Boetie, a few years older, was already known as a brilliant writer; as a student he had written a daring essay against tyranny, the Discourse on Voluntary Servitude. Montaigne says they had heard of each other before and that they were so taken with each other at that first meeting that from then on nothing was as close to either of them as the other.

Their friendship lasted only about four years. In August 1563 La Boetie fell ill with a fever and died at the age of thirty two, with Montaigne at his bedside. Montaigne wrote a long letter to his father describing his friend's last days.

Years later, when he retired to write his Essays, Montaigne devoted a chapter to friendship. He wrote that ordinary friendships are acquaintances held together by some interest, but in theirs two souls had blended so completely that the seam could not be found. If someone pressed him to say why he loved La Boetie, he could only answer: "Because it was he, because it was I." He also saw to it that his friend's writings were published.
lesson: The deepest friendships cannot be reduced to reasons or usefulness. When you find one, value it while you have it, because time together is never as long as you expect.
people: Michel de Montaigne, Etienne de La Boetie
source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book I, chapter 28, "Of Friendship"; Montaigne, letter to his father on La Boetie's death (1563)
